Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 70, verses 1–3:

﴿A questioner asked about a torment that is to befall﴾ Whoever reads "sa'ala" with a hamza (sa'ala) may take it in two senses. The first: it means supplication (du'a), i.e., a supplicant called down a torment that is to befall; this may refer to the words of the disbelievers, "Rain down upon us stones from the sky," and the one who said them was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The second: it means inquiry (istikhbar), i.e., a questioner asked about a torment that is to befall, and the "bi" here carries the sense of "'an" (about). This may refer to his saying: ﴿When will this promise be fulfilled?﴾ [Yunus: 48] and other such words. As for the one who reads "sal" without a hamza, it may be taken in two ways. The first: that it is a lightened form of the hamzated verb, so both of the meanings mentioned apply to it. The second: that it derives from "sala al-sayl" (the torrent flowed) when it runs, and this is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: "sala sayl" (a torrent flowed). In this case the "ba" is like your saying "dhahabtu bi-Zayd" (I went off with Zayd). When it derives from the torrent, it may be taken in two ways: the first, that the torment is likened to a torrent in its severity and the swiftness of its descent; the second, that it is literal. Zayd ibn Thabit said: "In Hell there is a valley called Sa'il." Thus it becomes clear that in the reading with a hamza there are two meanings, and in the reading without a hamza there are four meanings.

﴿for the disbelievers﴾ The "li" may be connected with "waqi'" (to befall), with the "lam" meaning "'ala" (upon); or it may be a qualifier of the torment; or it may be connected with "sa'ala" when that means "da'a" (called down), i.e., he called down a torment upon the disbelievers; or it may be a new sentence, as if he said: "It is for the disbelievers."

﴿from Allah﴾ It may be connected with "waqi'," meaning it befalls from the presence of Allah; or with "dafi'" (repeller), meaning there is no repeller for it from Allah; or it may be a qualifier of the torment, or a new sentence.

﴿Possessor of the ascents﴾ "Ma'arij" is the plural of "mi'raj," which is that by which one ascends to a height, like a ladder, and "al-madarij" are the steps by which one climbs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: here they are used figuratively for virtues and praiseworthy qualities. It was also said: they are the stairways to the heaven, and this is more apparent, because He explained them by what follows, namely the ascent of the angels.

And the Spirit ascends to Him: that is, to His Throne (al-‘Arsh), and from the place where His commands and decrees descend. So the ascent is from the earth to the Throne. If we say it is in this worldly life, then the meaning is that the angels and the Spirit ascend in a day which, if people ascended in it, would take them fifty thousand years. It has also been said that the fifty thousand years is the duration of this world, and the angels ascend and descend during this period. All of this is based on the premise that the phrase "in a Day" is connected to "ascend." It is also possible that "in a Day" describes the punishment, in which case the Day must be the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is consistent on this view.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 70, verses 5–10:

﴿So be patient﴾. This is connected to what precedes it, concerning the punishment and other matters. That is: be patient with the statements of the disbelievers until the punishment comes upon them. For this reason He described it as near, as an exaggeration in consoling the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed, they see it as distant﴾. It is possible that the pronoun refers to the punishment, or to the Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. "Distant" may mean distant in time or distant in possibility. Likewise, "near" may mean near in time, since everything that is coming is near, and because the Hour has drawn near; or near in possibility, given God's power over it. ﴿On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass (al-muhl)﴾. "The Day" here is either a substitute for the day whose measure is fifty thousand years, or a substitute for the object pronoun in (narahu) ("We see it"), or it is governed by "near" (qarīban), or by the words ﴿the criminal would wish﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], or by a hidden verb whose estimate is: remember. Al-muhl (molten metal, dregs) is the sediment of olive oil; the sky is likened to it in its blackness and the dimming of its lights on the Day of Resurrection. It is said that al-muhl is what has been melted of silver and the like, and the sky is likened to it in its changing colors. ﴿And the mountains will be like wool (al-ihn)﴾. Al-ihn is wool. The mountains are likened to it in their fluffiness and the looseness of their parts. It is said that al-ihn is wool dyed in various colors, so the comparison is in fluffiness and in the difference of colors, since the mountains are white, black, and red. ﴿And no intimate friend will ask of an intimate friend﴾. Al-hamim here means a close friend, and the meaning is that no one will ask his close friend for help or assistance, knowing that he has no power to provide anything. It is said that it means no one will ask about his condition, because each person is preoccupied with himself.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ It is said: بصر الرجلُ بالرجلِ (basara al-rajul bi-al-rajul) when he saw him, and بصَّرتُه إياه (basṣartuhu iyyahu) with the doubled ṣād when I showed him to him. The two pronouns (in ﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾, "they are shown them") refer back to al-ḥamīmān (the two close companions), because they carry the sense of a plural. The meaning is that every close friend will see his close friend on the Day of Resurrection and will recognize him, but he will not ask him anything. ﴿وَصَاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife. ﴿وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his nearest kin. ﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means "gathers him to herself," that is, she embraces him. This may mean that she embraces him in belonging to her, or in supporting him and protecting him from harms. ﴿ثُمَّ يُنجِيهِ﴾: its subject is the ransom that would be required if he were to ransom himself. This verb is conjoined to ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي﴾ (if he would ransom himself). He conjoined it with thumma (then) to signal the remoteness and impossibility of deliverance. For this reason He rebuked him with His saying ﴿كَلاَّ إِنَّهَا لَظَىٰ﴾ (No! Indeed it is the Blaze). The pronoun refers to the Fire, because the punishment indicates it. It may also be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa, the pronoun referring to the situation under discussion), explained by the following predicate. Ladhā (لظى) is a proper name for Hell, derived from al-laẓā (اللظى), meaning the flame. ﴿نَزَّاعَةً لِّلشَّوَىٰ﴾ (tearing away at the extremities). Al-shawā means the limbs of the body. It is also said to mean the skin of the head. The meaning is that the Fire tears them off and then they return. Nazzā'atan is in the nominative (marfū') as a substitute (badal) for laẓā, or as the predicate of an implied subject, or as the predicate of inna if we make laẓā a predicate of inna; it may be in the accusative as a specification (takhṣīṣ), or as a substitute for the pronoun, or as a second predicate of inna if we make laẓā its predicate. Nazzā'atan in the accusative is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). ﴿تَدْعُواْ مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ﴾ (It calls to him who turned his back and withdrew). This means the disbelievers who turned away from Islam. Its calling them is an expression of its seizing them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it calls them literally by their names and their fathers' names. It is also said that the meaning is that it destroys them, which al-Khalīl related from the Arabs. ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ﴾ (and gathered and hoarded). It is said: أوعيتُ المالَ وغيرَه (awʿaytu al-māla wa-ghayrahu) when I gathered wealth or other things into a container. So the meaning is that he gathered wealth and placed it in a container. This is an indication of a group of wealthy disbelievers who gathered wealth from unlawful sources and withheld its due right.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 70, verses 19–24:

﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious (haloo'an).﴾ Al-insan (mankind) here is a generic noun, as shown by the exception made from it. Ahmad ibn Yahya, author of al-Fasih, was asked about the word haloo' (anxious) and said: "Allah has explained it, and there is no clearer explanation than His explanation, which is His saying: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed (jazoo'an). And when good touches him, he is withholding (manoo'an).﴾" Allah mentioned these traits in a manner of blame, and for this reason He made an exception from them for those who pray, because their prayer leads them to little concern for worldly things, so they neither grieve over its evil nor withhold its good. ﴿Except those who are constant in their prayer (da'imoon).﴾ Constancy in it (al-dawam) is persistence in it throughout the length of one's life, and guarding it (al-muhafaza), mentioned after that, is performing it at its proper times and perfecting its purity (tahara) for it. ﴿A known right (haqqun ma'lum).﴾ We have already mentioned in al-Dhariyat [19] the meaning of haqq and of the beggar and the deprived. Here it is described as known. If it refers to zakat, then its amount is known by the Shari'ah. If it refers to other than zakat, then the meaning of "known" is that the servant places upon himself an obligation that is known to him.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Not to be secure against it﴾

Translation of the commentary:

"Not to be secure against it" means that no one should feel safe from it, for feeling secure from the punishment of God is forbidden (ḥarām). Therefore a servant should not remove fear from himself until he enters Paradise.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 70, verses 32–33:

﴿Who keep their trusts and their covenant﴾ is mentioned regarding the believers [8]. Likewise: ﴿and who are guardians of their chastity﴾. ﴿And those who stand firm in their testimonies﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." The majority (al-Jumhur) said: "It means testimony before judges."

Then they differed, on this view, regarding the meaning of standing firm in it (al-qiyam biha). It was said: it is verifying it (al-tahqiq laha), as in his saying ﷺ (ﷺ): "Upon the like of the sun, then bear witness." It was also said: it is hastening to give it without hesitation. As for the witness who is called to give testimony, it is obligatory upon him. As for when he is not called to give it, testimony falls into three categories:

First: the rights of people, so it is not permissible to give it until the person with the right calls him to do so.

Second: the rights of Allah in which the prohibition remains continuous, such as divorce (al-talaq), manumission (al-ʿitq), and endowments (al-ahbas). Giving testimony regarding these is obligatory whether or not one is called.

Third: the rights of Allah in which the prohibition does not remain continuous, such as the hudud (prescribed punishments). This should be concealed until one is called to it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 70, verses 36–39:

﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, rushing towards you [O Muhammad]﴾, meaning hastening towards you, coming to you with their eyes fixed. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came, the disbelievers would look at him and listen to his recitation. The meaning of "qibalaka" is "in your direction and what is in front of you." ﴿Groups scattered﴾, meaning separate clusters. It is the plural of ʿizah, with the zay lightened, and its original form is ʿizwah. It is said that it was originally ʿizhah, then its final radical was dropped and it was pluralized with the waw and nun as a substitute for the dropped radical.

﴿Does every one of them aspire to enter a Garden of bliss?﴾ They used to say: if there is indeed a Garden, then we are its people. ﴿No!﴾ This is a rebuke to them for what they aspired to, namely entering Paradise. ﴿Indeed, We created them from that which they know﴾, a metaphor for the semen from which Allah created man. There are three views regarding the intended meaning of this statement. The first: belittling man and refuting the arrogant. The second: a refutation of the disbelievers in their hope to enter Paradise, as if He is saying: "We created you from the same thing from which We created people, so no one enters Paradise except through righteous deeds, because you are equal in your creation." The third: an argument for resurrection, that Allah created them from a despised water, so He is able to restore them, as in His saying: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37], to the end of the surah.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 70, verses 40–43:**

﴿So I swear not﴾: its meaning is "I swear," and the "lā" is extra (*zā'idah*). ﴿by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾. This is mentioned in Surah al-Saffat [37:5]. ﴿Indeed, We are able * to replace them with better than them﴾: this is a threat to the disbelievers with their destruction and the replacement of them with something better. ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾, that is, not overcome. The meaning is: We are not incapable of the replacement mentioned or of the resurrection. ﴿So leave them﴾: this is a warning to them. In it is a truce (*muhadanah*) that was abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the sword. ﴿until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾: this means the Day of Resurrection, as shown by the fact that the following phrase is a substitution for it: ﴿the Day they emerge from the graves﴾, which are the tombs, ﴿as if they were rushing toward a shrine (*nusub*), hastening﴾. The *nusub* are idols. Its original meaning is anything set up (*nusiba*) toward which a person heads quickly, whether a flag, a building, or something else. There are dialectal readings of it: opening the *nūn* with the *ṣād* sukun, and the *nūn* with a *ḍammah* and the *ṣād* with sukun, and the *ḍammah* on both. *Yūfiḍūn* means they hasten. The meaning is that they will hasten out of the graves to the place of gathering, just as they used to hasten to walk to their idols in this world.
